intro: Long ago, some people joined groups that kept a secret. In Greece, thousands walked to a town called Eleusis for holy rites. They promised never to tell what they saw. In the Roman world, small groups of men met in dark, cave-like rooms to honor a god named Mithras. In southern Italy, a teacher named Pythagoras led a brotherhood that loved numbers.

These groups left very little writing about their secrets. So how do we know anything about them? We look at old buildings, floors, carvings and poems. We read what visitors and enemies wrote. Then we sort what is well supported from what is only a legend.

In this unit, you will walk the Sacred Way, climb the seven steps of Mithras and try a Pythagorean number rule. By the end, you will be able to explain why people joined these groups. You will also be able to use evidence to tell a fact from a story told later.
bigQuestion: How can we learn the truth about ancient groups that worked hard to keep their secrets?

timeline.t: The Hymn to Demeter tells the story of Demeter, Persephone and the rites at Eleusis.
Pythagoras leads a brotherhood of followers at Croton, in southern Italy.
Athens is upset when young men are accused of acting out the Mysteries at parties.
A woman named Ninnion gives a painted clay tablet to the goddesses of Eleusis.
The travel writer Pausanias visits Eleusis but will not describe what is inside.
A mithraeum is built in Rome, in the place where San Clemente church stands today.
The London Mithraeum is built beside the Walbrook river.
The Felicissimus mithraeum at Ostia gets its seven-grade mosaic floor.
Emperor Theodosius makes a law against the old rites. The Mysteries soon end.
Diggers find the mithraeum deep beneath the church of San Clemente in Rome.
Archaeologists find the marble head of Mithras on the last day of a dig in London.
The rebuilt London Mithraeum opens to visitors.

words.d: a person who has joined a group through a special ceremony
the secret rites held at Eleusis, open only to people who had joined
a holy place with temples and altars, set apart from everyday life
a large group of people walking together for a special reason
a serious promise, often made in a holy way
the high priest of Eleusis; the name means one who shows the holy things
a small, cave-like room where followers of Mithras met
a rank or level in a group; members move up from one grade to the next
a picture made of many small pieces of stone or glass set close together
a close group of people who treat each other like family and share rules
a story told for a long time that cannot be proven true
facts or objects that help show what is true

test.q: Which goddess of grain was honored at Eleusis?
test.why: The Mysteries of Eleusis honored Demeter, goddess of grain, and her daughter Persephone.

test.q: What did every initiate at Eleusis promise?
test.why: Every initiate made a vow of silence about what was shown and said inside the hall.

test.q: About how long was the walk from Athens to Eleusis?
test.why: The Sacred Way from Athens to Eleusis was about 13 miles long.

test.q: In what building did the most secret rites at Eleusis take place?
test.why: The Telesterion was the huge hall at Eleusis where the secret rites happened.

test.q: Why did the Mysteries of Eleusis end in the late 300s CE?
choices: Roman laws closed the old rites and the sanctuary was wrecked
test.why: In 392 CE Emperor Theodosius passed a law against the old rites, and in 396 CE the sanctuary was wrecked.

test.q: Which is the best reason the secret of Eleusis is still unknown?
choices: The Ninnion Tablet shows it all
Pausanias told it in his book
Initiates kept their promise of silence
test.why: Initiates kept their vow, and even writers like Pausanias stopped before telling it.

test.q: What were the rooms where followers of Mithras met like?
choices: Small, dark rooms made to feel like caves
test.why: Mithraea were small, dark, cave-like rooms with benches along the sides.

test.q: Which kinds of people joined the groups of Mithras?
choices: Men such as soldiers, traders and enslaved or freed workers
test.why: Most scholars think only men joined; many were soldiers, and others were traders, officials, and enslaved or freed men.

test.q: What does the Felicissimus floor at Ostia show?
choices: The seven grades of Mithras members
A map of the Sacred Way
test.why: The mosaic floor has seven panels, one for each grade, with symbols and planets.

test.q: How are the Ninnion Tablet and the Felicissimus mosaic alike?
choices: Both show the final secret of Eleusis
Both are pictures that give clues about secret groups
test.why: The tablet gives clues about Eleusis, and the mosaic gives clues about the grades of Mithras.

test.q: What happened in London on 18 September 1954?
choices: The marble head of Mithras was found
The Ostia floor was dug up
test.why: On the last planned day of the Walbrook dig, the team found the marble head of Mithras.

test.q: What did later writers say new Pythagorean members had to do?
choices: Stay silent and listen for a long time
test.why: Later writers say new members stayed silent for a long time, some say five years, before speaking.

test.q: What does Plimpton 322 teach us about the Pythagorean theorem?
choices: The rule was known in Babylon long before Pythagoras
It was found under San Clemente
It was a secret of Eleusis
test.why: The Babylonian tablet lists number sets that fit the rule, more than a thousand years before Pythagoras.

test.q: Which of these is a legend?
choices: Hippasus was punished for sharing a math secret
The London Mithraeum was found in 1954
The Mysteries ended in the late 300s CE
test.why: The Hippasus story comes only from late writers with no earlier record, so historians call it a legend.

test.q: Why do historians read Tertullian and Clement of Alexandria with care?
choices: They opposed the religions they wrote about
test.why: Both were Christian writers who opposed these religions, so their reports may be one-sided.

write.prompt: Which group kept its secrets better: the initiates of Eleusis, the followers of Mithras, or the Pythagoreans? Make a claim. Use two or three facts or sources from this unit to support it, and explain your thinking.
tips: Start with one clear sentence that states your claim.
Name your sources, such as the Hymn to Demeter, Pausanias, the Ostia floor or Polybius.
Say what we know for sure and what is only a legend.
Use unit words like initiate, vow, mithraeum and evidence.
Be fair: say one thing the other groups did well, too.
